conflicts: AARO's 19 November 2024 SASC case slides assess GO FAST as showing an object at roughly 13,000 feet moving at about 45 mph with 60-knot winds, i.e. 'did not demonstrate any anomalous speeds or flight characteristics.' Graves's testimony does not rest on GO FAST's speed but on the near-midair in W-72 and the absence of a reporting mechanism, neither of which AARO's parallax analysis addresses.

label: Ryan Graves
narrative: Graves converted the 2014-2015 USS Theodore Roosevelt workup encounters from an anecdote into an institutional safety problem, which is why he is the aviator the disclosure movement could not be talked out of. In his written statement to House Oversight on 26 July 2023 he testified: 'In 2014, I was near Virginia Beach as part of VFA-11, a Navy Fighter/Attack Squadron made up of F/A-18F Super Hornets,' and that his squadron 'began witnessing advanced UAP demonstrating complex maneuvers on a regular basis' after the fleet upgraded to the APG-79 AESA radar. The pivotal event he described occurred in Warning Area W-72, 'an exclusive block of airspace ten miles east of Virginia Beach,' where 'one of the pilots saw a dark gray cube inside of a clear sphere - motionless against the wind, fixed directly at the entry point,' and two jets 'only 100 feet apart, were forced to take evasive action.' The institutional failure is the part that indicts: 'Our squadron submitted a safety report, but there was no official acknowledgement of the incident and no further mechanism to report the sightings.' Two of the three videos the Department of Defense formally released on 27 April 2020 - GIMBAL and GO FAST, both filmed in January 2015 - came out of this operating area. Graves founded Americans for Safe Aerospace to build the reporting channel the Navy did not provide, telling Congress in July 2023 that it had 'nearly 5,000 members' and was 'actively working with more than 30 UAP witnesses.'
